title: Free fall in a vacuum

relationships: gravity produces force proportional to mass

visual_plan.goal: Show two masses accelerating equally when air resistance is absent

visual.title: Equal acceleration in a vacuum
visual.description: Conceptual motion diagram showing both objects covering increasing distances by the same acceleration pattern.
visual.alt_text: Two objects of different masses fall side by side inside a vacuum chamber with equal downward acceleration arrows.

explanation.visual_intuition: The objects have different weights, but the heavier object also needs proportionally more force to produce the same acceleration.
explanation.how_it_works: Gravity provides F=mg. Newton's second law gives F=ma. Equating them gives ma=mg and therefore a=g.
explanation.why_it_works: Mass appears on both sides and cancels. With negligible air resistance, acceleration depends on the gravitational field, not the object's mass.
explanation.worked_example: If the local gravitational acceleration is approximately 9.8 m/s², both objects have approximately that acceleration regardless of mass.
explanation.verification: The units of acceleration remain m/s² and the result is independent of mass.

equations.meaning: free-fall acceleration in the ideal vacuum model

assumptions: The gravitational field is approximately uniform over the experiment.
verification: Both sides have consistent force units before cancellation.
misconceptions: A heavier object does not automatically have greater gravitational acceleration in the ideal vacuum model.
key_takeaway: In a vacuum, different masses fall with the same gravitational acceleration because the gravitational force and inertial resistance both scale with mass.
